content.content:
# GitHub App Callback URLs

**Maximum URLs:** A GitHub App can register "up to 10 callback URLs."

**Multiple Redirect URIs:** Yes, you can add multiple callback URLs. When doing so, use the `redirect_uri` parameter to specify which URL the user should be directed to following authorization. "If you do not specify a `redirect_uri`, the first callback URL will be used."

**Matching Rules:** Two modes are available:

1. **Exact Matching (Default):** The redirect URL must match the callback URL precisely.

2. **Wildcard Matching (Optional):** When enabled, the host and port must match exactly, but the path can reference any subdirectory of the callback URL. This allows "any subdomain or subdirectory of the callback URL" to work as valid redirect destinations.

⚠️ **Security Note:** Wildcard matching poses risks by potentially allowing attackers to redirect authorization codes to uncontrolled subdomains or paths. Enable it only if necessary and you control all possible subdomains and paths involved.

# OAuth Device Flow and PKCE Support

**Does the device flow require a client secret?**

No. The documentation states: "For the device flow, you must pass your app's client ID, which you can find on your app settings page. The `client_secret` is not needed for the device flow."

**Does GitHub support PKCE for the authorization code flow?**

Yes. GitHub supports PKCE with the authorization code grant type. The web application flow accepts `code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method` parameters, both marked as "strongly recommended."

**Are the OAuth endpoints usable from a browser (CORS)?**

No. The documentation explicitly notes: "CORS pre-flight requests (OPTIONS) are not supported at this time."

**About client secrets and web flow:**

"The client secret you received from GitHub for your OAuth app" must be submitted when exchanging an authorization code for an access token in the web application flow.

- [ ] **Register a GitHub App** ([new App](https://github.com/settings/apps/new)) with read-only **Contents**, **Issues** and **Actions**, and *Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation* enabled. Callback URL: the deployed dashboard's page URL — or the `https://<user>.github.io/` root with **Enable wildcard matching** ticked, which covers every future deployment on that host. ## "Revalidated" vs "floored", in TTL terms

Three cache classes, and only one of them ever had a TTL:

**Immutable** — keyed by commit sha (`contents?ref=<sha>`, the tree). TTL is infinite *by construction*: content at a sha cannot change, so there is nothing to go stale and nothing to ask about.

**Revalidated (ETag)** — effectively **TTL = 0**. The page asks every single time, but sends `If-None-Match: <etag>`. If nothing changed GitHub answers `304`, empty body — and [a 304 does not count against the primary rate limit](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api). So it is never stale and nearly free *in quota* — but it is still an HTTP round trip: latency you wait for, and a request against the *secondary* limit (100 concurrent, 900 points/minute), which is counted in requests **made**, not budget spent. That is the gap the old design had: a warm fleet reload cost 0 quota and 50 round trips.

**Floored (`minAge`)** — the new part, and the plainest way to say it: **the floor turns a revalidated entry into a TTL entry, with the TTL chosen per load from your remaining budget.** Below the floor the page does not ask at all — no request, not even the conditional one — and accepts data up to `minAge` old. Above it, revalidation resumes as before.

| Data | live | tight | low | scarce | frozen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| content at a sha | ∞ | ∞ | ∞ | ∞ | ∞ |
| repo, head sha, runs, open queue | 0 (revalidate) | **5m** | **30m** | **until reset** | until reset |
| settled issue history | 24h | 3d | 7d | 30d | 30d |
| requests a warm reload makes | ~1 per entry (all 304) | 0 within 5m | 0 within 30m | **0** | **0** |

So "floored at 30m" reads exactly as "a 30-minute TTL, applied to things that otherwise have none". One consequence worth knowing: under a floor, **Reload** obeys it — **Clear cache** is the override.

## #1003 — once, or once per fleet?

**Once, ever.** One App and one exchange serve every deployment. I've rewritten [#1003](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1003) to say so:

- a GitHub App carries **up to 10 callback URLs**, and with **wildcard matching** a single `https://missingbulb.github.io/` callback covers every project Pages site on that host — so a new Shepherd adds *no* callback;
- installation is per **account**, not per repo;
- the exchange holds the App's secret and nothing else, so one deployment serves all;
- the only per-fleet step is pasting the same two config keys. They stay config rather than a pack default deliberately — a client ID names *your* App, and canon code naming one deployment is the coupling `canonRepo` is config to avoid.

## The secret swap without running anything — no

The docs state "CORS pre-flight requests (OPTIONS) are not supported at this time", and a browser cannot read a response carrying no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` regardless. I could not probe the token endpoint's actual headers — this sandbox's proxy denies `github.com/login/*` — so that second half is documented rather than measured here.

**The Chrome extension case is genuinely different**, which is why it felt server-free: an extension with host permissions is not bound by a page's CORS rules, so it calls the token endpoint itself. Two ways to get one:

- **Sign in with GitHub** — a button, no typing. Available when the deployment
  configures `clientId` and `exchangeUrl`.
- **A pasted token** — the fallback, and the local-development path. Needs
  read-only **Contents**, **Issues** and **Actions**.

### What each credential is worth

The reason sign-in is not a nicety. GitHub's limits, per hour:

| Credential | Limit |
|---|---|
| unauthenticated | **60**, per IP address |
| a user token — PAT, OAuth, or a GitHub App user token | **5,000**, shared across every app acting for that user |
| a GitHub App *installation* token | 5,000 minimum, up to 12,500 by size |
| an Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` | 1,000, per repository |

A twelve-member sweep costs around 75 requests cold. So an unconfigured deployment —
no `clientId`, nobody pasting a token — exceeds the whole anonymous hour on its
**first load**, and 5,000/hour is not an optimisation over that, it is 83×. There is
no higher tier available to a page that runs as its viewer: an installation token
would raise the ceiling, but only by putting a shared credential behind a backend,
which would show every viewer everything that app can see. That is a different
product, not a bigger limit.

### Why "just use my existing GitHub login" is not on that list

input.body:
Four steps no Action can take — they need a credential and a console. Until all four are done the dashboard runs **unauthenticated at 60 requests/hour per IP**, which one fleet sweep exceeds. Context in #996.

**Scope: once per fleet *owner*, not once per fleet — and not once for everybody.** One App and one exchange endpoint serve every deployment *you* own. A GitHub App carries [up to 10 callback URLs](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/registering-a-github-app/about-the-user-authorization-callback-url), and with **wildcard matching** a single callback of `https://<user>.github.io/` covers every project Pages site under that host — so a new Shepherd for a new fleet of yours adds no callback at all, just the two config keys.

Somebody else adopting this pack cannot inherit it, for mechanical reasons: a private App "can only be installed on the account that owns the app. Only members of the organization that owns it can authorize it", and even a public one yields a user token that "can only access resources that both the user and app can access" — so until they install it themselves their whole fleet reads *not visible to you*, and their tokens would be minted by someone else's endpoint. They register their own, or use the token box. Spelled out in the pack README (#1007).

- [ ] **Register a GitHub App** ([new App](https://github.com/settings/apps/new)) with read-only **Contents**, **Issues** and **Actions**, and *Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation* enabled. Callback URL: the deployed dashboard's page URL — or the `https://<user>.github.io/` root with **Enable wildcard matching** ticked, which covers every future deployment on that host. Note the **client ID**, generate a **client secret**.
  - *while undone:* no sign-in button exists; every viewer is anonymous.
- [ ] **Install the App** on the account holding the fleet's repos ([installations](https://github.com/settings/installations)). Once per *account*, not per repo — a new repo under an installed account is covered by "all repositories", or added to the selection.
  - *while undone:* sign-in succeeds but the token can read nothing, so every member row reads "not visible to you".
- [ ] **Deploy the exchange** — [`oauth-exchange.example.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/claudinite-dashboard/oauth-exchange.example.mjs) as-is to a worker, with the client ID and secret as its environment. One deployment serves every dashboard you own, since it holds that App's secret and nothing else.
  - *while undone:* clicking sign-in returns to a page that cannot finish, and says the exchange was unreachable.
- [ ] **Set `clientId` and `exchangeUrl`** on the deployment's `claudinite-dashboard` entry in its `.claudinite-checks.json`. Either alone does nothing — the pair is what turns sign-in on. This is the one step a new fleet of yours repeats, with the same two values.
  - *while undone:* nothing changes; the page keeps falling back to the token box.

**Closing condition:** the deployed dashboard shows *Sign in with GitHub*, one authorization gets a viewer through a full fleet sweep, and the rate pill reads `…/5000 · user`.

### Why the exchange cannot be skipped

Verified against the [authorizing-OAuth-apps docs](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps):

- the web flow's token exchange lists `client_secret` as **Required**, flatly — GitHub supports PKCE (`code_challenge`, S256 only) but as *additional* protection, not as a public-client mode that drops the secret;
- the device flow genuinely needs no secret ("The `client_secret` is not needed for the device flow") but it POSTs to `github.com/login/device/code` and `github.com/login/oauth/access_token`, and those are cross-origin for a page on `github.io`. The docs state "CORS pre-flight requests (OPTIONS) are not supported at this time"; a browser cannot read a response that carries no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` either. *(The response headers of the token endpoint could not be probed from this sandbox — the proxy denies it — so that last half is documented, not measured here.)*

A browser extension is the case where this *does* work without a server, which is why the Chrome extension flow felt server-free: an extension with host permissions is not subject to the page's CORS rules, so it can call the token endpoint itself. A static page has no such exemption.

This is not a wider credential in each member repo — the App acts as whoever signed in, with exactly their own permissions.

Two things #1003 got wrong by being a hand-written issue in one repo.

**Adoption never handed the sign-in work over.** `adoptionHandover` carried the Pages setting and nothing else, so every future adopter met the gap as "why is my dashboard rate-limited" — the failure mode the field exists to prevent. It now carries a second entry, and a real `install.mjs` run prints both:

```
install: 2 step(s) only a human can do — open a tracking issue for these:
  [ ] (claudinite-dashboard) Enable GitHub Pages …
  [ ] (claudinite-dashboard) Decide how this dashboard authenticates its viewers …
        while off: … a viewer who has not pasted a token reads GitHub anonymously at 60 requests/hour per IP …
        done when: a signed-in viewer sees the rate pill read "…/5000 · user", or this repo has recorded that
                   the token box is this deployment's answer
```

**One entry, not four checkboxes** — deliberately. A member reading its own repo through a pasted token has *nothing to do*, at the identical 5,000/hour, so four unconditional steps would be mostly no-ops, which is what teaches a reader to skim the list that exists to stop them skimming. The decision is what every adopter owes; the README now carries the four mechanics in the order they unblock each other.

**"Register once, ever" was under-qualified** — true across one owner's deployments, wrong across owners, and an adopter is exactly who would assume otherwise. The README says which reuse works and why the other cannot:

- one owner, many deployments — up to ten callback URLs, wildcard matching covers every project Pages site on one `github.io` host, so a new deployment copies two config keys;
- a different owner — a private App "can only be installed on the account that owns the app. Only members of the organization that owns it can authorize it"; a public one lets them authorize, but a user access token "can only access resources that both the user and app can access", so until they install it their fleet reads *not visible to you*. And then their callback would live in someone else's App and their tokens be minted by someone else's endpoint — a trust relationship, not a config knob.

Quotes verified against [generating a user access token](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-a-user-access-token-for-a-github-app) and [app visibility](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/registering-a-github-app/making-a-github-app-public-or-private), read from the fetched pages rather than summarised.
